title: A word said twice
where: *Othello*, Act 3, Scene 3; Act 4, Scene 1; Act 5, Scene 2
about: Othello, a Moor and a general of Venice, has married Desdemona, a senator’s daughter. Iago, his ensign, wanted the lieutenancy that Othello gave to Michael Cassio, and is working to make Othello believe that Cassio and Desdemona are lovers. In the first passage Iago begins, soon after Cassio has been seen leaving Desdemona; in the second he tells Othello that Cassio has talked; in the third Othello stands over his sleeping wife, come to kill her.

view.says: Auden compares Iago to an analyst with a patient, except that this one works to kill. Iago never has to lie, Auden says, because everything he tells Othello is meant to bring to the surface what is already in Othello’s mind. Even where a plain lie would be safe, Iago gives an answer that can be taken two ways and leaves the taking to Othello.
view.quote: his answer is equivocal and its interpretation is left to Othello
view.source: “The Joker in the Pack,” in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962), p. 266
view.checked: read in the scan of The Dyer’s Hand, research/auden/dh.txt, lines 12695-12717, on 2026-10-03

lenses.label: Figure
lenses.name: anadiplosis
lenses.plain: a doubling back: the word that ends one sentence begins the next
lenses.why: Iago hands Othello’s words back as questions and commits himself to nothing; the monster, and the conclusion that Iago means something, come from Othello, as in Auden’s account, where Iago need only bring up what is already in Othello’s mind.
lenses.caption: A word ends one speech and begins the next: indeed, then honest, then think. Rhetoric calls this anadiplosis, a doubling back, and here the doubled word changes speakers. Iago speaks four times, thirteen words in all. Three of the four are questions, and two of those are Othello’s last word handed back with my lord. Iago’s one statement goes no further than for aught I know. Auden writes that Iago never has to lie, because what he says is meant to bring up what is already in Othello’s mind. It is Othello who names the device, he echoes me, who says monster, and who concludes that Iago means something.

grounds.claim: which words come back, who says them, and how much Iago says
anadiplosis is beginning a sentence or clause with the last, or a prominent, word of the one before; the Greek means a doubling back
grounds.source: A New English Dictionary on Historical Principles, vol. I (1888), under Anadiplosis

lenses.label: Beat
lenses.meterName: ten syllables and five beats, the line beginning off the beat, without rhyme

points.say: Two syllables, one beat. Othello’s reply is a full line without it.
Eleven syllables. Othello says Iago’s word back and then answers it. *Ay* can be heard as a sixth beat.

The Folger edition prints Iago’s six syllables and these four as one line of ten. The Globe edition makes its line of ten from this question and the three words said twice after it. A Victorian grammar of Shakespeare’s English has a name for a part-line that ends one line and begins the next: *amphibious*.
Iago’s three words again. Here they begin a line of five beats, which starts on a beat and counts *heaven* as one syllable. The Globe edition gives these three words to the line before.

lenses.why: Shakespeare breaks the five-beat line into short pieces here; in his verse a line left short can mark a pause, and Othello soon calls Iago’s pauses stops and says they frighten him the more.
lenses.caption: The first line is whole: ten syllables, five beats. Iago’s Indeed? has two syllables and one beat. After another full line six short pieces follow, none longer than six syllables. Editions join them into lines differently. The Folger and Globe editions both print Iago’s Indeed? alone, and each leaves other pieces short. In Shakespeare’s verse a line left short can mark a pause. A dozen lines on, Othello calls Iago’s pauses stops and says they frighten him the more.

lenses.why: The word Iago hands back names the virtue that, as Auden told his class, Othello prizes and Iago sees as the key to him; and the monster, Auden writes, is a fear already in Othello’s own mind.
lenses.caption: Honest and honesty have been said twenty-one times before this line, twelve of them about Iago, and never yet to ask whether someone is honest. Here Othello asks it of Cassio. Auden told his class that Othello sets great store by simple virtues such as honesty, and that Iago sees this is the key to him. The word could also mean chaste, and later in the scene Othello says it of his wife, in doubt. The noun monster is first heard here, from Othello; Iago takes it up later for jealousy. Auden reads it as Othello’s own fear: that Venice values him only for his use.

lenses.why: Shakespeare gives Iago a word that is two verbs, so the answer can be taken two ways and, as Auden says, the taking is left to Othello, whose prose finds both senses, names slander, and returns to the bed.
lenses.caption: Iago’s answer is one syllable, and two verbs share it: to lie down and to tell a lie. Asked With her? he gives two prepositions and what you will. Auden quotes these lines: even here, where a plain lie would be safe, the answer can be taken two ways and the taking is left to Othello. Othello takes it both ways. Lie with her is the bed. Lie on her, he says, is said when they belie her, when lies are told about a woman. He has named slander, and he goes back to the bed: fulsome, foul. When Othello has fallen in a trance, Iago’s own word for such women is guiltless.

lenses.label: Figure
lenses.name: antimetabole
lenses.plain: the same words said again in the opposite order
lenses.why: Othello turns the proverb round so that hanging comes before confession: he ordered Cassio’s death in Act 3, before he heard of these confessions, and for him, Auden says, what Desdemona has or has not done no longer matters.
lenses.caption: Confess and be hanged was a proverb. The Oxford dictionary says it appears to have been a degree ruder than saying you lie. Othello says it of Cassio, then turns it round: hanged first, confess after. In the play the death sentence has come first: Othello orders Cassio’s death in Act 3, and what he here calls Cassio’s confessions he first hears of in this scene. In Act 5 Othello tells his wife to confess and, in the same speech, that she is to die. Once Othello doubts her love, Auden writes, it no longer matters what she has or has not done.

grounds.claim: the two halves of the saying and the order in which Othello puts them the second time

lenses.why: The longest run of whole sentences in the speech is Othello’s reasoning about his own shaking, where he says words are not its cause; on Auden’s account Iago’s words are meant to bring up what is already in Othello’s mind.
lenses.caption: Iago has said eight words since Othello’s What? What? Othello answers with seventy-four. He begins by saying Iago’s phrases back, and he ends in pieces of one to four words: Noses, ears, and lips. Near the end three whole sentences stand together, and they are about himself. He trembles. Nature, he says, would not put on such passion without some instruction: without some prompting, as the lexicon of Shakespeare’s words explains it. What shakes him, he says, is not words. Auden’s account is that Iago’s words are meant to bring up what is already in Othello’s mind. After the last piece the stage direction is Falls in a trance.

Iago has used both forms since the first scene: 2,431 words of prose, most of them to Roderigo and to Cassio. lenses.label: Figure
lenses.name: antanaclasis
lenses.plain: the same words said again with a different meaning
lenses.why: The line gives two acts the same four words, and the next six lines draw the difference themselves: the flame can be lit again if he repents, and for her light he does not know where the fire is.
lenses.caption: One line says the same four words twice. The first time they mean the flame burning in the room, the second time her life. Nothing in the line itself marks the change; the six lines after it do. He speaks first to the flame, thou flaming minister, then to her, thou cunning’st pattern of excelling nature, and the word light comes back three times, once as the flame’s and twice as hers. The flame’s he can restore, should I repent me. For hers he does not know where the fire is that can.

lenses.why: Shakespeare builds the two sentences alike, condition, address, the verb placed last, and changes who can: over the flame it is Othello, and over his wife a fire he does not know where to find.
lenses.caption: Two sentences are built to one plan. Each begins with a condition: If I quench thee, But once put out thy light. Each turns aside to name the one spoken to, the flame in three words and the woman in a whole line. In each the thing acted on comes before its verb, so the verb comes last: restore ends its clause and relume its sentence. The end of a sentence is usually its place of most weight. The two differ in who can. In the first sentence it is I. In the second it is a fire, and he does not know where it is.

grounds.claim: the matching parts of the two sentences, and the place of each verb

lenses.why: He says cause three times and will not name it, as in Act 4, where, Auden notes, his charges are nameless; the word itself could mean a reason, a lawsuit or a charge.
lenses.caption: He says cause three times and will not name it. The word meant a reason, a lawsuit, sometimes a charge. Auden writes that what exactly she has done no longer matters to Othello: in Act 4 he charges her with nameless things, not with adultery with Cassio. Here too nothing is named, and the one reason given is more men. Monumental alabaster is the stone of a tomb, of the figure placed over a grave, and he says it of a sleeping woman’s skin.

grounds.claim: he says cause three times, will not name it, and says she must die or she will betray more men; she is asleep

grounds.claim: cause: a reason or motive; in law, a case; sometimes a charge or accusation

auden.says: Auden begins from the villain. He can think of no other play in which one character alone does deeds and all the rest only show behavior: every act in it is Iago’s. Othello’s fall, he writes, is another man’s work, so that an audience pities Othello without respecting him and keeps for Iago the respect Auden calls aesthetic.
auden.quote: nothing he says or does originates with himself
auden.source: “The Joker in the Pack,” in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962), pp. 246–47
auden.checked: read in the scan of The Dyer’s Hand, research/auden/dh.txt, lines 11695-11727, on 2026-10-03

auden.says: Auden asks the actor of Iago for the greatest contrast between Iago in company and Iago alone. With others he should show every skill a great actor has, and be a different honest man for each person he talks to: one for Roderigo, one for Cassio, one for Othello, one for Desdemona. Alone, he should speak his soliloquies badly, pausing where the verse asks for no pause and stressing words that do not matter. The reason Auden gives is that what Iago wants in the end is nothingness, for the others and for himself.
auden.source: “The Joker in the Pack,” in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962), p. 258
auden.checked: read in the scan of The Dyer’s Hand, research/auden/dh.txt, lines 12277-12300, on 2026-10-03

auden.says: At the end of Act 3, Scene 3, Othello tells Iago he is now his lieutenant, and Iago answers that he is Othello’s own for ever. Auden calls the answer a mocking repetition of a line Othello spoke earlier, and reads *lieutenant* here as a private and unlawful commission, to have Cassio killed in secret, and no public rank. He does not say which line he means. Earlier in the scene Othello tells Iago that he is bound to him for ever.
auden.source: “The Joker in the Pack,” in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962), p. 249

auden.says: Donald Pearce took the class in 1941 and wrote down what he could afterward. His notes say that the lectures on Shakespeare were mostly about the minds of the characters and the society around them, and hardly touched the verse or the rhetoric, though Auden asked the class to read Wilson Knight, who does. Auden called Othello deliberately naive, a man who lays great stress on simple virtues such as honesty, and said that Iago sees this is the key to him. Iago he called the one brilliant mind in the play: cold, unable to love, reasoning without a flaw, moving other people like pieces in a game.
auden.source: Donald Pearce, “Fortunate Fall: W. H. Auden at Michigan,” in *W. H. Auden: The Far Interior*, edited by Alan Bold (1985), pp. 139 and 142–43
auden.checked: read in research/A_pearce_gap2.txt, a copy of these pages kept with the research scans, and in remake/research/E_pd_pearce.md, on 2026-10-03; the pages are missing from research/auden/pearce.txt

auden.says: Pearce’s notes give six diagrams that Auden put on the blackboard for the lecture on *Othello*. Each sorts the people of the play: by rank, by self-confidence, by sex appeal, by passion, by sophistication, by intelligence. The last sets Iago alone as intelligent and the rest as stupid. Charles Miller, another student in the class, remembered the diagrams as meant to prove Othello a stupid man and Iago more honest than anyone else in the play. Miller adds that he and other students were put off by what looked like flippancy about Shakespeare.

caveats: What Auden told his class in 1941 is known from notes that a student, Donald Pearce, made after the lectures. It is not Auden’s own text. Charles Miller’s sentence about the blackboard was seen only in search results from a scanned copy of his book.

Auden’s sentence that Iago never has to lie goes further than the play. In [Act 3, Scene 3](#/read/othello/a3s3:319) Iago says he saw Cassio wipe his beard with the handkerchief that day, when he has it himself. And that Cassio has talked, in the second passage, rests on Iago’s word alone.

Editions divide the short speeches of the first passage into lines differently. The Folger and the Globe do it as the Beat tab says; the Cambridge edition of 1866 prints each speech by itself. The stresses marked on the short pieces can be heard in more than one way.

The counts of verse and prose follow the text printed here, which prints Othello’s *With her?* in the second passage as prose. The Folger edition sets those two words in a verse line. Counted that way, his prose comes to 358 words, not 360.

Two early printings differ: the Quarto of 1622 lacks the long speech of the second passage from *To confess* onward, and has another word for *relume*. In the first passage the Folio of 1623 has *thou* for *he*. The Globe edition prints Iago’s three short speeches there with exclamation marks.
open: Auden’s sentence that Iago need not lie goes further than the play does. In Act 3, Scene 3 Iago says he saw Cassio wipe his beard with the handkerchief that day, which is untrue. In Act 5, Scene 2 he says he told Othello no more than what Othello himself found apt and true, and a moment later admits he told him that Desdemona was false. The first passage shows him committing himself to nothing. In the second he reports that Cassio has said he did something, which rests on his word alone (the examiner’s item below). The passages do not show that he never lies.

Pearce’s pages 137 to 145 are missing from the scan research/auden/pearce.txt. They were read in another copy kept with the research files (A_pearce_gap2.txt) and in the research summary E_pd_pearce.md. The page numbers given follow the page numbers printed in that copy. What Pearce gives is a student’s notes made after the lectures, not Auden’s own text.

The hosted text prints Othello’s two words at Act 4, Scene 1, block 45 as prose, and the counts follow it. The Folger edition sets them as part of a verse line, so that his prose begins two words later, with the long speech. Counted that way from the hosted text, his prose comes to 358 words.

The second half of the long speech on the second plate, from the proverb to the end, stands in the 1623 Folio and not in the 1622 Quarto, by the marks in the Folger edition. In the first passage, where the hosted text has Othello speak of Iago as he, the 1623 Folio and the Folger edition have him say thou. On the third plate relume is the Folio’s word; Schmidt’s lexicon records that the 1622 Quarto has return there, and that the Quartos have cunning where the plate has cunning’st.

Editions divide the short speeches of the first plate into lines in different ways; the Beat tab gives the Folger’s and the Globe’s, in its caption and, since the critic’s changes, more fully in its third and fourth remarks. The Cambridge edition of 1866, by the Globe’s editors, prints each of them as a line by itself. The plate scans each speech as the hosted text prints it, and the scansion of the short pieces can be heard in more than one way. The notes give the other hearings.
The question marks after Iago’s three short speeches on the first plate are those of the hosted text, the 1623 Folio and the Folger edition. The Globe edition prints exclamation marks there.

The two dictionaries do not gloss fulsome alike for the second plate: the Oxford dictionary gives this line as its first example of morally foul, obscene; Schmidt’s lexicon puts it under disgusting, nauseous.

From the examiner: Auden’s sentence on p. 266 about what Iago’s words are designed to do has a pronoun that can be read two ways. What is brought to Othello’s consciousness is either what Iago has guessed is there or what Othello has guessed. The analyst of Auden’s comparison is Iago, which favors the first. The poet had written the second as if it were certain. The view, two captions and two reasons now say only what both readings share: it is already in Othello’s mind.

From the examiner: inside the second passage Iago does say something untrue. At row 39.0, after block 35, he reports that Cassio has said he did something, and does not say what. Later in the same scene (block 80, rows 10 to 12) he says that he will make Cassio tell again where, how often and when he has had Othello’s wife and is to have her again. The second caveat had said that the first two passages show only that he commits himself to nothing. It now says that Cassio’s talk rests on Iago’s word alone.

From the examiner: the Figure caption of the second passage said that the first talk of a confession comes in Act 4. Forms of confess are spoken seven times before that scene, of other people and other things, once by Iago to Cassio himself (Act 2, Scene 3, block 214), and in Act 3 Iago reports what Cassio said in his sleep. The caption now says only that Othello orders Cassio’s death in Act 3 and first hears in this scene of what he calls Cassio’s confessions.

From the examiner: the two counts of prose speeches in the facts of the Play tab were counts of prose blocks, 24 and 82. A speech is defined there as one turn under a speaker’s name, and four turns hold two prose blocks each. Counted as turns they are 23 and 79, and the facts now say so. The artist’s drawing prints these two numbers from the same keys.

From the examiner: the Figure and Sentence tabs of the second passage stand on words that are only in the 1623 Folio (row 49.0 from word 19 to the end), by the marks in the Folger edition. The fifth caveat tells the reader. A lead who wants only words that both early texts share would have to drop these two tabs.

From the examiner: the checker’s one warning is on Othello’s own word at row 112.0, word 6, quoted in italics in the Figure caption of the first passage. The sentence says only that he names the device. It was left.

From the examiner: my own scansion of the first passage differs from the poet’s in the weight of single words at rows 100.0 (word 1), 100.1 (word 0), 104.0 (word 1), 108.0 (word 0), 112.0 (word 7) and 112.2 (words 6 and 7). Either hearing can be defended. The captions rest only on the counts of syllables, which are the same both ways.
